Triangular lattice models of the Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin liquid from coupled wires

Tingyu Gao (高廷宇) Affiliation: Department of Condensed Matter Physics, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot 7610001, Israel Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of Cologne, D-50937 Köln, Germany    Niklas Tausendpfund Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of Cologne, D-50937 Köln, Germany Affiliation: Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Quantum Control, Peter Grünberg Institut (PGI-8), 52425 Jülich, Germany    Erik L. August 24, 2026
Abstract

Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) are exotic phases of interacting spins in two dimensions, characterized by long-range entanglement and fractional excitations. We construct a local Hamiltonian on the triangular lattice that stabilizes the Kalmeyer-Laughlin CSL without requiring fine-tuning. Our approach employs coupled-wire constructions and introduces a lattice duality to construct a solvable chiral sliding Luttinger liquid, which is driven toward the CSL phase by generic perturbations. By combining symmetry analysis and bosonization, we make sharp predictions for the ground states on quasi-one-dimensional cylinders and tori, which exhibit a fourfold periodicity in the circumference. Extensive tensor network simulations demonstrating ground-state degeneracies, fractional quasiparticles, nonvanishing long-range order parameters, and entanglement signatures confirm the emergence of the CSL in the lattice Hamiltonian.

I Introduction

Interacting spins on a lattice typically realize ground states that break internal symmetries, such as spin rotations or lattice symmetries. Competition between interactions that favor different ordering patterns can result in enhanced quantum fluctuations that instead promote quantum spin liquids; see Refs. [3, 67, 91, 82, 4] for recent reviews. These strongly correlated states are characterized by topological order instead of symmetry-breaking and exhibit long-range entanglement.

The Kalmeyer-Laughlin chiral spin liquid (CSL) [38] is a paradigmatic example of this class of phases. It shares many qualitative features with fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, particularly, the ν=1/2\nu=1/2 Laughlin state of bosons [43]. Both phases exhibit a topological degeneracy on a torus, chiral edge states at an open boundary, and fractional quasiparticles that exhibit anyonic exchange statistics. Microscopically, the FQH and CSL differ significantly regarding the relevant length scales and their competition with other phases. Quantum Hall states are most easily realized in continuous systems or at low densities where the interparticle spacing is the only relevant length scale. By contrast, quantum spin liquids are governed by lattice scale effects and compete energetically with conventional, symmetry-broken phases. Consequently, finding generic lattice Hamiltonians whose ground states realize spin liquids represents a significant challenge.

For the Kalmeyer-Laughlin CSL, Refs. [68, 76, 60] addressed this challenge by constructing a Hamiltonian that explicitly projects onto a specific many-body wave function representing this phase. A less direct but more widely applicable route involves “coupled wire” constructions. This approach was pioneered for FQH states in Ref. [39] and adapted for CSLs in Refs. [53, 23]. It begins by analytically solving decoupled one-dimensional subsystems (wires) using field-theory techniques. Carefully selected couplings between the wires are then introduced into the effective field theory to form a two-dimensional phase.

In this article, we combine the coupled-wire approach with tensor-network methods [87, 90] to introduce a local Hamiltonian (up to four-spin terms) for the CSL on the triangular lattice and confirm its ground state. The crucial step in our approach is the construction of the gapless sliding Luttinger liquids (SLL) with the CSL as the strongest instability. The SLL fixed point is characterized by a separate U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry for each wire in the array. Such symmetry requirement is, however, not a sufficient condition for having an SLL. In general, even interchain interactions that preserve these U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries induce instabilities to gapped phases that preempt the formation of the SLL. Here, we employ a duality relation to identify nonperturbative interwire couplings that realize the SLL fixed point with certainty. Moreover, we can analytically control the universal parameters of the SLL through the coupling constant of local lattice operators.

Our analysis of the coupled-wire model reveals how the CSL manifests itself in quasi-one-dimensional systems. In particular, we analyze the quasi-one-dimensional avatars of the topologically degenerate sectors expected in two dimensions. On cylinders formed by NN wires, we find a surprising fourfold periodicity. When NN is not a multiple of four, the one-dimensional ground state exhibits weak symmetry breaking [80] with an order parameter that vanishes exponentially with NN. When NN is a multiple of four, the one-dimensional ground state is unique and symmetric. In this case, the different topological sectors of the two-dimensional phase correspond to different symmetry-protected topological (SPT) states in one dimension, which become degenerate as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty.

We tested the detailed predictions based on the coupled wire analysis using extensive numerical simulations. The ground states obtained from density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) [87] and variational uniform matrix product state (VUMPS) [90] techniques on narrow-width (finite and infinite) cylinders confirm the expected signatures of quasi-one-dimensional CSL avatars. In particular, we investigated ground-state degeneracies, symmetry breaking, string order parameters, entanglement spectra, and spin pumping. Additionally, we employed infinite projected-entangled pair states (iPEPS) [79, 35] to show that, by use of variational optimization [12, 48, 58], we can find a chiral spin liquid state in the proposed model and characterize it via its entanglement spectrum.

This article is organized as follows: In Sec. II, we briefly review the essential aspects of the Kalmeyer-Laughlin CSL and how to construct it from coupled wires. In particular, we discuss the relevant symmetries and identify competing phases, such as valence bond solids and antiferromagnets. In Sec. III, we engineer a lattice model for the SLL and derive its field theory using a combination of duality and one-dimensional bosonization. In Sec. IV, we analyze CSL signatures in the quasi-one-dimensional limit. Section V presents our numerical results, which support a CSL ground state. We conclude in Sec. VI with a brief discussion of our main results and possible generalization to more exotic spin liquids.

II Chiral spin liquid and coupled-wire construction

Spin systems in two or higher dimensions usually settle into conventional, symmetry-breaking phases, such as valence bond solids, antiferromagnets, or ferromagnets. However, it is now well established that symmetry-preserving but topologically ordered phases are also possible [3, 67]. Such states may form when frustration between different interactions enhances quantum fluctuations and suppresses conventional orders. A prominent example of frustration occurs when spins interact anti-ferromagnetically on the triangular lattice. The three spins at the corners of each triangular plaquette cannot be simultaneously antiparallel to both of their neighbors. Consequently, the resonating valence bond state—a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quantum spin liquid in modern parlance—was proposed as a possible ground state [67].

Seminal work by Kalmeyer and Laughlin revealed an intimate connection between frustrated spin models and quantum Hall systems [38]. Spin-exchange interactions are mathematically equivalent to hopping processes and interactions of hard-core bosons. The frustration translates into a non-zero background flux for these bosons. On the triangular lattice, this flux is π\pi per triangular plaquette. Summing these fluxes yields a total phase of 2​π2\pi per unit cell. In the zero magnetization sector, where the bosons are at half-filling of the lattice, the Landau-level filling factor is ν=1/2\nu=1/2, allowing the bosons to form a Laughlin state.

The ground state of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice was later shown to be in a Néel state [6, 86]. Still, the Kalmeyer-Laughlin CSL is an energetically competitive state that could be stabilized by additional next-nearest-neighbor or multispin interactions. References [68, 76] built on the quantum Hall connection to construct exact parent Hamiltonians for the Kalmeyer-Laughlin wave function. Soon after, Ref. [60] proposed another exact model by studying a modified wave function in light of conformal field theory. In particular, this model can be truncated into a short-range Hamiltonian consisting of two- and three-spin interactions that realize the same phase [61].

Here, we pursue a different strategy based on a perspective that originates in fractional quantum Hall studies. Coupled-wire models have become a popular theoretical tool for analytically capturing topological states of electrons, bosons, or spins [39, 75, 53, 23]. They do not yield exact microscopic Hamiltonians like the ones in Refs. [68, 76, 60]. However, in return, they offer much broader applicability.

II.1 Coupled-wire construction of quantum Hall states and chiral spin liquids

The main idea behind the coupled-wire description of chiral topological states is shown in Fig. 1. Its starting point is an array of electronic quantum wires or spin chains in the gapless phase, governed by the Hamiltonian density

ℋLL​[φ,θ]=u2​π​[1K​(∇θ)2+K​(∇φ)2]\mathcal{H}_{\text{LL}}\left[\varphi,\theta\right]=\frac{u}{2\pi}\,\left[\frac{1}{K}\left(\nabla\theta\right)^{2}+K\left(\nabla\varphi\right)^{2}\right] (1)

of each wire. It is written in terms of two conjugate bosons, which obey the commutation relation [∂xφ⁡(x),θ⁡(x′)]=i​π​δ​(x−x′)\commutator{\partial_x \varphi(x)}{\theta(x')}=i\pi\delta(x-x^{\prime}). The two fields are equivalent to a pair of left- and right-moving modes ϕL/Rn=φ±n​θ\phi^{n}_{L/R}=\varphi\pm n\theta, which decouple when the Luttinger parameter K=1/nK=1/n.

Quantum Hall states or chiral spin liquids arise when left- and right-moving modes on neighboring wires gap out in pairs, leaving unpaired chiral modes at the boundary. To achieve such a topological state, the array must be coupled via a relevant perturbation in the renormalization group (RG) sense. A low-energy operator that can induce a chiral state is given by

𝒪chiraln=cos⁡[ϕL,yn−ϕR,y+1n],\displaystyle{\cal{O}}_{\text{chiral}}^{n}=\cos[\phi^{n}_{L,y}-\phi^{n}_{R,y+1}]\penalty\ , (2)

where yy labels the wires, and nn must be even (odd) for spins (fermions). In the case of continuous translations in xx, this operator is only kinematically allowed to appear in the Hamiltonian in a magnetic field corresponding to the filling factor ν=1/n\nu=1/n. The scaling dimension of 𝒪chiraln{\cal{O}}_{\text{chiral}}^{n} according to ℋ0=∑yℋLL​[φy,θy]{\cal H}_{0}=\sum_{y}{\cal H}_{\text{LL}}[\varphi_{y},\theta_{y}] is

Δn​(K)=12​K+n22​K,\displaystyle\Delta_{n}(K)=\frac{1}{2K}+\frac{n^{2}}{2}K\penalty\ , (3)

whose minimum is minK⁡Δn​(K)=n\min_{K}\Delta_{n}(K)=n (for K=1/nK=1/n). The decoupled array is invariant under a rescaling of time and the wire direction xx but not the transverse direction yy. Consequently, an operator is relevant if the scaling dimension Δ<2\Delta<2. For spin systems, nn must be even; the CSL with the smallest Δ\Delta thus occurs for n=2n=2 and will be our focus. In the decoupled array, it can, at best, be marginal (at K=1/2K=1/2).

Gapped phases accessed via marginally relevant perturbations would exhibit small energy gaps and large correlation lengths, which are obstacles to efficient numerical studies. Moreover, competing phases driven by more relevant operators can preempt the flow toward the CSL and result in a different ground state. The possible competing phases are dictated by the lattice structure, and we focus on the triangular lattice for its built-in frustration.

Before closing, we note that for a chiral state without fractionalization, the integer quantum Hall state of bosons at ν=2\nu=2 [49, 20, 69, 17], the corresponding interwire coupling can be tuned relevant by intrawire couplings alone. Specifically, the interwire coupling cos⁡(φy+1−2​θy−φy−1)\cos(\varphi_{y+1} - 2 \theta_{y} -\varphi_{y-1}) has scaling dimension ΔBIQH​(K)=12​K+K\Delta_{\text{BIQH}}(K)=\frac{1}{2K}+K, with the minimum ΔBIQH​(1/2)=2\Delta_{\text{BIQH}}(1/\sqrt{2})=\sqrt{2}. Under this condition, the connection between coupled-wire analysis and lattice models is relatively straightforward, as discussed in Refs. [16, 27].

II.2 Symmetries and competing phases on a triangular array

We consider a triangular array defined by fundamental lattice vectors 𝒃0=x^\bm{b}_{0}=\hat{x} and 𝒃±=12​x^±32​y^\bm{b}_{\pm}=\frac{1}{2}\hat{x}\pm\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{y}, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The six-fold rotation symmetry is broken in the anisotropic limit of coupled wires, and we retain only translation and parity (mirror) symmetries. To realize the CSL, we break the time-reversal symmetry (𝒯)({\cal T}) and the mirror symmetry (𝒫)({\cal P}) while preserving their product. We also relax the SU(2) spin rotation symmetry and require only invariance under arbitrary rotations around SzS^{z} and under a π\pi rotation around SxS^{x}. The latter symmetry implies an unpolarized state with ⟨Sz⟩=0\langle S^{z}\rangle=0, equivalent to the half-filling of hard-core bosons. The discrete symmetries are summarized in Tab. 1.

The spin Hamiltonian

H∥\displaystyle H_{\parallel} =12​∑𝒓(S𝒓+​S𝒓+𝒃0−+H.c.)+J∥z​∑𝒓S𝒓z​S𝒓+𝒃0z\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{r}}\left(S^{+}_{\bm{r}}S^{-}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{0}}+\text{H.c.}\right)+J^{z}_{\parallel}\sum_{\bm{r}}S^{z}_{\bm{r}}S^{z}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{0}}\penalty\ (4)

describes an array of decoupled chains, each of which realizes Eq. (1) for J∥z∈(−1,1)J^{z}_{\parallel}\in(-1,1). The parameters u,Ku,K are known from the Bethe ansatz solution to be [21]

H⟂\displaystyle H_{\perp} =J⟂2∑i=±∑𝒓(S𝒓+S𝒓+𝒃i−+H.c.)\displaystyle=\frac{J_{\perp}}{2}\sum_{i=\pm}\sum_{\bm{r}}\left(S^{+}_{\bm{r}}S^{-}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{i}}+\text{H.c.}\right) (7a)

When inserting Eq. (6b) into the second line, the oscillatory contributions from S𝒓+S^{+}_{\bm{r}} and S𝒓+𝒃0+S^{+}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{0}} cancel. We thus obtain

ℋ⟂∼g​∑y[𝒪chiral+𝒪antichiral]+⋯,{\cal H}_{\perp}\sim g\sum_{y}\,[{\cal O}_{\text{chiral}}+{\cal O}_{\text{antichiral}}]+\cdots\penalty\ , (8)

For example, the operator 𝒪X​Y{\mathcal{O}}_{XY} can lead to a striped phase with antiferromagnetic order along xx and ferromagnetic order along yy between every two chains. One approach to quantify the competition is to compare the scaling dimensions. For the competitors above, we find

In particular, at the value K=1/2K=1/2, where the perturbation 𝒪chiral{\cal{O}}_{\text{chiral}} is (marginally) relevant, two strongly relevant perturbations drive the system into competing phases. Figure 3 shows all four dimensions for KK in the interval (0.5,1.2)(0.5,1.2). Therefore, to achieve the desired ν=1/2\nu=1/2 CSL, we resort to a different starting point, which we detail in the next section.

III Chiral sliding Luttinger liquid

To promote the CSL, we would like to access it via a relevant perturbation and simultaneously suppress the competing phases. Both can be achieved by generalizing the decoupled array to a coupled one that realizes a SLL fixed point at low energy [39]. The main challenge to constructing a suitable SLL is that generic interwire couplings often drive the wire array into one of the competing symmetry-broken phases. We overcome this difficulty first by designing interwire couplings that maintain integrability, which we prove below using a duality relation. The key ingredient for the SLL is the spin rotation operator

R𝒓α≡e−i​π​α​S𝒓z=cos⁡((π2​α))−2​i​S𝒓z​sin⁡((π2​α)),R_{\bm{r}}^{\alpha}\equiv e^{-i\pi\alpha S^{z}_{\bm{r}}}=\cos{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \alpha\right)}-2iS^{z}_{\bm{r}}\sin{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \alpha\right)}\penalty\ , (12)

which rotates the spin at the site 𝒓\bm{r} by π​α\pi\alpha counterclockwise around the zz axis in the spin space. In addition, we include perturbative couplings between wires for further optimization.

The lattice Hamiltonian we propose consists of two contributions, HCSLL=H♢​(α)+HZZ​(J∥z,J⟂z)H_{\text{CSLL}}=H_{\diamondsuit}(\alpha)+H^{\text{ZZ}}(J^{z}_{\parallel},J^{z}_{\perp}), with

Crucially, this Hamiltonian conserves SzS^{z} on each wire separately. For noninteger α\alpha, it contains three-spin terms such as S𝒓+𝒃+z​(S→𝒓×S→𝒓+𝒃0)zS_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{+}}^{z}\left(\vec{S}_{\bm{r}}\times\vec{S}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{0}}\right)^{z} that break time-reversal 𝒯{\cal T} and parity 𝒫{\cal P} symmetries, and are known to enhance quantum fluctuations and promote spin-liquid behavior [83, 22, 23, 11].

We emphasize that all these scaling dimensions are perturbative in λ\lambda but exact in α\alpha.

The scaling dimension of 𝒪antichiral\mathcal{O}_{\text{antichiral}} in Eq. (8) follows from changing the sign of α\alpha in Eq. (16). In particular, it becomes less relevant for positive α\alpha. However, we note that

𝒪antichiral′=cos⁡((2​θy−1+2​θy+2−φy+φy+1)){\cal O}^{\prime}_{\text{antichiral}}=\cos{\left(2\theta_{y-1} + 2\theta_{y+2} - \varphi_y + \varphi_{y+1}\right)}\penalty\ (18)

realizes a CSL with the same chirality as 𝒪antichiral{\cal O}_{\text{antichiral}} and is favored by positive α\alpha. Moreover, it is also generated at first order in J⟂J_{\perp}. At leading order in λ\lambda, its scaling dimension is related to that of 𝒪chiral{\cal O}_{\text{chiral}} via

Δantichiral′−Δchiral=λ​K​(1−α).\Delta^{\prime}_{\text{antichiral}}-\Delta_{\text{chiral}}=\lambda K\left(1-\alpha\right)\penalty\ . (19)

At λ=0\lambda=0, the two scaling dimensions coincide. Still, the two operators are unrelated by symmetries and thus generically occur with different bare coupling constants that will select one chirality over the other. In our work, we use positive λ\lambda to reduce the value of Δchiral\Delta_{\text{chiral}}, which additionally suppresses the opposite chirality.

III.1 Integrability of the sliding Luttinger liquid

Two-leg ladder models similar to H♢H_{\diamondsuit} of Eq. (13a) were introduced and studied in Refs. [66, 65]. Specifically, Ref. [65] solved it using a nonlocal unitary transformation, akin to the Kennedy-Tasaki transformation [40, 62]. Similarly, we introduce a set of nonlocal spin 1/2 operators S~\tilde{S} with S~z=Sz\tilde{S}^{z}=S^{z} and

S~𝒓−\displaystyle\tilde{S}^{-}_{\bm{r}} ≡[∏n=1∞R𝒓−n​𝒃−α]​S𝒓−​[∏n=1∞R𝒓+n​𝒃−α],\displaystyle\equiv\left[\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}R^{\alpha}_{\bm{r}-n\bm{b}_{-}}\right]S_{\bm{r}}^{-}\left[\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}R^{\alpha}_{\bm{r}+n\bm{b}_{-}}\right]\penalty\ ,
≡[⋯RαRαS𝒓−RαRα⋯].\displaystyle\equiv\begin{bmatrix}\cdots&R^{\alpha}&R^{\alpha}&&&\\ &&&S^{-}_{\bm{r}}&&\\ &&&&R^{\alpha}&R^{\alpha}&\cdots\end{bmatrix}\penalty\ . (20)

Here, each RαR^{\alpha} is the rotation operator of Eq. (12). The second line illustrates the spatial structure of the string operators, which extend to ±∞\pm\infty on the neighboring wires (all operators in the bracket are multiplied). The interaction in Eq. (13a), which includes terms on a ‘diamond’ for four sites (Fig. 4), maps onto an intrawire spin exchange in the dual variables, i.e.,

[RαS𝒓+S𝒓+𝒃0−Rα†]=S~𝒓+​S~𝒓+𝒃0−.\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}&R^{\alpha}&\\ S_{\bm{r}}^{+}&&S_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{0}}^{-}\\ &R^{\alpha\dagger}&\end{bmatrix}=\tilde{S}^{+}_{\bm{r}}\tilde{S}^{-}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{0}}\penalty\ . (21)

Consequently, Eq. (13a) describes X​YXY chains of dual spins

H♢​[S~]=12​∑𝒓S~𝒓+​S~𝒓+𝒃0−+H.c.\displaystyle H_{\diamondsuit}[\tilde{S}]=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{r}}\tilde{S}^{+}_{\bm{r}}\tilde{S}^{-}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{0}}+\text{H.c.}\penalty\ (22)

Since the spin zz component is unaltered in Eq. (20), the coupled array HCSLLH_{\text{CSLL}} of microscopic spins SS is thus equivalent to a decoupled, integrable array of dual spins S~\tilde{S} [Eq. (4)] when |J∥z|<1|J^{z}_{\parallel}|<1 and J⟂z=0J^{z}_{\perp}=0. Consequently, the long-wavelength behavior of this two-dimensional spin system is encoded in a sum of ℋLL\mathcal{H}_{\text{LL}} in Eq. (1) with non-local field variables θ~y,φ~y\tilde{\theta}_{y},\tilde{\varphi}_{y}, which are related to S~\tilde{S} as in Eqs. (6a) and (6b).

To obtain the effective field theory in Eq. (15), it remains to relate θ~y,φ~y\tilde{\theta}_{y},\tilde{\varphi}_{y} to θy,φy\theta_{y},\varphi_{y}. From here on, we take α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) without loss of generality because H♢H_{\diamondsuit} is invariant under α→α+2\alpha\rightarrow\alpha+2, and time-reversal relates positive and negative α\alpha. First, Sz=S~zS^{z}=\tilde{S}^{z} implies θ=θ~\theta=\tilde{\theta}. Second, bosonizing the string operator using the non-oscillating first term in Eq. (6a), we get

∏m=0∞R𝒓+m​𝒃0α\displaystyle\prod_{m=0}^{\infty}R^{\alpha}_{\bm{r}+m\bm{b}_{0}} =exp[−iπ∑m=0∞αS𝒓+m​𝒃0z]\displaystyle=\exp\left[-i\pi\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\alpha S^{z}_{\bm{r}+m\bm{b}_{0}}\right] (23)
∼r0​e−i​α​θ~y​(x)+(−1)x​rπ​e−i⁡(α−2)​θ~y​(x),\displaystyle\sim r_{0}e^{-i\alpha\tilde{\theta}_{y}(x)}+(-1)^{x}r_{\pi}e^{-i\left(\alpha-2\right)\tilde{\theta}_{y}(x)},

with nonuniversal constants r0,πr_{0,\pi}. For α<1\alpha<1, which we assumed, we drop the second term as less relevant than the first. Inserting Eq. (23) into Eq. (20) and using Eq. (6b), we conclude that

φy≡φ~y−α​θ~y−1+α​θ~y+1,θy≡θ~y,\varphi_{y}\equiv\tilde{\varphi}_{y}-\alpha\tilde{\theta}_{y-1}+\alpha\tilde{\theta}_{y+1},\qquad\theta_{y}\equiv\tilde{\theta}_{y}, (24)

as claimed in Eq. (14). Using this relation on an array of Luttinger liquids described by Eq. (1) in θ~,φ~\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\varphi}, we arrive at Eq. (15) with λ=0\lambda=0.

In Fig. 5, we show the scaling dimensions of the CSL and other competitors as functions of α\alpha by fixing the parameter KK. For additional details about the duality transformation and some numerical tests, see Appendix A.

Physically, the duality transformation is closely related to flux attachment. Specifically, Eq. (24) is a truncated version of the transformation introduced in Refs. [55, 56] to transform electrons or bosons into composite fermions. A crucial distinction is that the transformation used in the current work is only non-local in the xx direction and thus maps H♢H_{\diamondsuit} onto a local model. Still, the scaling dimensions in Eqs. (11) and (16) show that, for sufficiently large α\alpha, it favors “composite fermion states” such as the CSL—an integer quantum Hall state of composite fermions—over more conventional phases of the microscopic spins.

III.2 Perturbative interwire couplings

Perturbative interwire couplings can further optimize the SLL fixed point toward CSL instabilities. One example is to include two-body spin-zz interactions in the vertical direction, i.e., the first term in Eq. (13b). In the perturbative regime where J⟂z≪1J_{\perp}^{z}\ll 1, using the bosonization dictionary Eq. (6a) immediately yields the last term in the low-energy effective Hamiltonian of Eq. (15). Beyond the perturbative regime, the correct fixed point includes additional symmetry-allowed terms, such as (∂xθy)​(∂xθy+2)\left(\partial_{x}\theta_{y}\right)\left(\partial_{x}\theta_{y+2}\right) [71]. Nevertheless, we expect Eq. (15) to remain a reasonable approximation to the effective Hamiltonian until J⟂zJ^{z}_{\perp} of order unity, which is confirmed by the numerical results shown in Appendix B.

The scaling dimensions at the fixed point defined by Eq. (15) are shown in Fig. 6 for the choice of J∥z=−0.1J^{z}_{\parallel}=-0.1 and α=0.75\alpha=0.75. When the number of wires NN is finite, we implicitly assume a periodic boundary condition in the transverse direction. We observe that the additional parameter λ\lambda further reduces the scaling dimension of the 𝒪chiral{\cal O}_{\text{chiral}} and separates it from its antichiral counterpart in the two-dimensional limit. More details about calculating the scaling dimensions can be found in Appendix C.

IV Precursors of the chiral spin liquid in quasi-one-dimension

Coupled-wire systems with a finite number of chains NN, strictly speaking, are only quasi-one-dimensional. Therefore, no topological orders should occur [8]. Nevertheless, the bosonized formulation provides a straightforward route for finding unique properties associated with the one-dimensional descendants of the CSL. In those phases, the arguments of the cosines in 𝒪chiral{\cal O}_{\text{chiral}} are pinned to

2​θy+2​θy+1+φy−φy+1=(2​ny+1)​π,2\theta_{y}+2\theta_{y+1}+\varphi_{y}-\varphi_{y+1}=(2n_{y}+1)\pi, (25)

with integer nyn_{y}, assuming a positive coupling for 𝒪chiral\mathcal{O}_{\text{chiral}} in the field theory. (For the opposite sign in front of the cosine, the pinned values are even multiples of π\pi). Since the system is periodic in the transverse direction, the equation implies

Θ≡∑y=1Nθy=N4​π+π2​∑yny.\displaystyle\Theta\equiv\sum_{y=1}^{N}\theta_{y}=\frac{N}{4}\pi+\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{y}n_{y}\penalty\ . (26)

Microscopic operators local in the xx direction (but not necessarily in yy) must be invariant under the shift θ→θ+π\theta\rightarrow\theta+\pi; see Eqs. (6a) and (6b). The simplest physical operator that acquires an expectation value when Θ\Theta is pinned is 𝒪Θ≡e2​i​Θ{\cal O}_{\Theta}\equiv e^{2i\Theta}, which serves as an order parameter later on. Its two possible expectation values characterize distinct ground states for which the sum in Eq. (26) is either odd or even.

IV.1 Spin pumping via flux insertion

A hallmark of CSLs (FQHs) is that inserting a flux quantum is associated with accumulating a fractional spin (charge) excitation. We encode flux threading the cylinder through the boundary condition of the vertex field ei​φye^{i\varphi_{y}} in the transverse direction. In particular, changing the flux by Φ\Phi amounts to

φN−φ1→φN−φ1+Φ.\displaystyle\varphi_{N}-\varphi_{1}\rightarrow\varphi_{N}-\varphi_{1}+\Phi\penalty\ . (27)

Making this replacement in Eqs. (25) and (26), we find that adiabatically inserting a full flux quantum, Φ=2​π\Phi=2\pi, results in

δ​Θ2​π=π2.\displaystyle\delta\Theta_{2\pi}=\frac{\pi}{2}\penalty\ . (28)

The induced change of the spin in an interval IR⁡(L)I_{R(L)} that encompasses the right (left) cylinder boundary but is smaller than the cylinder length is given by

δ​SR⁡(L)z\displaystyle\delta S^{z}_{R(L)} =∑(x,y)∈IR⁡(L)Szx,y∼−1π∫IR⁡(L)∂xδΘ2​π=±12.\displaystyle=\sum_{(x,y)\in I_{R(L)}}S^{z}_{x,y}\sim-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{I_{R(L)}}\partial_{x}\delta\Theta_{2\pi}=\pm\frac{1}{2}\penalty\ . (29)

Here, we used SzS^{z} of Eq. (6a) and that Θ\Theta outside the cylinder is pinned to a value that is insensitive to the flux insertion (Formally, one can model the trivial vacuum as an intrawire VBS state on each chain).

We emphasize that this argument does not make any assumption on NN and thus holds equally when N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. However, it does require a bulk energy density that is the same for Θ\Theta and Θ+π/2\Theta+\pi/2. In two-dimensional limits, these two values encode different topological sectors. We now address the meaning of the two ground states in the quasi-one-dimensional regime.

IV.2 Degenerate ground states

Our main findings are summarized in Table 2. First, the two degenerate ground states may reveal themselves as symmetry-broken states in quasi-one-dimension, which can be inferred by the symmetry action on the vertex operator 𝒪Θ{\cal O}_{\Theta}. The symmetry properties of the vertex operator follow from the transformation of θ,φ\theta,\varphi, summarized in Table 1. We find

Tx​𝒪Θ​Tx−1\displaystyle T_{x}{\cal O}_{\Theta}T_{x}^{-1} =(−1)N​𝒪Θ\displaystyle=(-1)^{N}{\cal O}_{\Theta}\quad (any N) ,\displaystyle\text{(any $N$) },
Π​𝒪Θ​Π−1\displaystyle\Pi{\cal O}_{\Theta}\Pi^{-1} =𝒪Θ†\displaystyle={\cal O}^{\dagger}_{\Theta}\quad (any N) ,\displaystyle\text{(any $N$) }, (30)
𝒫𝒯𝒪Θ​(𝒫𝒯)−1\displaystyle{\cal PT}{\cal O}_{\Theta}({\cal PT})^{-1} =(−1)N/2​𝒪Θ\displaystyle=(-1)^{N/2}{\cal O}_{\Theta}\quad (even N only),\displaystyle\text{(even $N$ only)},

where the symmetry 𝒫𝒯{\cal PT} is only defined for an even number of wires with suitable boundary conditions (Fig. 2). In particular, the translation symmetry is broken for any odd NN, while 𝒫𝒯{\cal PT} is broken for N=2,6,10,…N=2,6,10,\ldots.

When NN is an integer multiple of four, all symmetries are preserved in the ground state. We argue that two SPT states, possibly one trivial and one nontrivial, become degenerate in such arrays. The symmetries in Eq. (30) imply that

ℋΘ=gΘ​cos⁡2​Θ\displaystyle{\cal H}_{\Theta}=g_{\Theta}\cos 2\Theta (31)

is an allowed perturbation in such arrays and selects a ground state with either Θ=0\Theta=0 or Θ=π/2\Theta=\pi/2, depending on the sign of gΘg_{\Theta}. Microscopically, gΘg_{\Theta} arises from a string of spin operators wrapping around the cylinder and is thus exponentially suppressed in the circumference. Consequently, the energy splitting between the Θ=0\Theta=0 and Θ=π/2\Theta=\pi/2 states is also exponentially small.

The analysis done in Eq. (29) implies that domain walls between the two states trap a total spin SDWz=±12S^{z}_{\text{DW}}=\pm\frac{1}{2}. Symmetry-protected boundary modes of this type are a signature of SPT phases, such as the Haldane phase [24, 1, 13, 40, 41]. We note that our lattice model HCSLL+H⟂H_{\text{CSLL}}+H_{\perp} is invariant under rotation by π\pi along any two perpendicular axes in the spin space, and the same ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry protects the Haldane phase in the spin-1 chain [40, 62, 64].

IV.3 String order parameters

Nonlocal observables involving string operators discussed in Eq. (23), i.e.,

syβ​(x)≡∏m=0xRm​𝒃0β∼e−i​β​θy​(0)+i​β​θy​(x)s^{\beta}_{y}(x)\equiv\prod_{m=0}^{x}R^{\beta}_{m\bm{b}_{0}}\sim e^{-i\beta\theta_{y}(0)+i\beta\theta_{y}(x)} (32)

can provide additional evidence of a CSL ground state. In particular, we find that the product of the operators over all wires with cylindrical boundary conditions satisfies

⟨∏ysyβ​(x)⟩∼⟨e−i​β​Θ​(0)+i​β​Θ​(x)⟩=e−β22​⟨[Θ⁡(0)−Θ⁡(x)]2⟩,\begin{split}\expectationvalue{\prod_y s^\beta_{y}(x)}\sim\expectationvalue{e^{-i \beta\Theta(0)+i \beta\Theta(x)}}=e^{-\frac{\beta^{2}}{2}\expectationvalue{ \left[\Theta(0)-\Theta(x)\right]^2}}\penalty\ ,\end{split} (33)

which has a finite x→∞x\rightarrow\infty limit for the CSL since Θ\Theta is pinned. However, since the system is fully gapped, the expectation value of each individual syβs_{y}^{\beta} (or any of their products) decays exponentially unless θy\theta_{y} is pinned, i.e., unless the yyth chain is in a VBS or Ising state. The analysis shows that expectation values of different string operators can provide a clear signature of quasi-one-dimensional CSL precursors.

For open boundary conditions in the yy direction, Eq. (8) contains one fewer cosine than for periodic boundaries. Consequently, Eq. (25) holds for N−1N-1 terms only. Summing these terms, we find

4​Θ=∑y=1N−1(2​ny+1)​π+(2​θN+φN+2​θ1−φ1).4\Theta=\sum_{y=1}^{N-1}(2n_{y}+1)\pi+(2\theta_{N}+\varphi_{N}+2\theta_{1}-\varphi_{1}). (34)

The additional terms on the right-hand side describe gapless edge excitations at the y=1y=1 and y=Ny=N boundaries. These edge modes result in a universal power law decay of the spin-spin correlations along the boundary, given by ⟨S0,y+​Sx,y−⟩∼x−2\langle S^{+}_{0,y}S^{-}_{x,y}\rangle\sim x^{-2} for y=1y=1 or y=Ny=N. Similarly, we find that the string operator for a system with open boundaries exhibits a slow power-law decay

⟨∏ysyβ​(x)⟩OBC∼1xβ2/4.\begin{split}\expectationvalue{\prod_y s^\beta_{y}(x)}_{\text{OBC}}\sim\frac{1}{x^{\beta^{2}/4}}\penalty\ .\end{split} (35)

V Tensor network simulations

The lattice Hamiltonian for realizing the CSL is a sum of H⟂H_{\perp} of Eq. (7a) and HCSLLH_{\text{CSLL}} of Eqs. (13a) and (13b). For our simulations, we choose the parameters

α=0.75,J∥z=−0.1,J⟂z=0.4\displaystyle\alpha=0.75\penalty\ ,\quad J^{z}_{\parallel}=-0.1\penalty\ ,\quad J^{z}_{\perp}=0.4\penalty\ (36)

in HCSLLH_{\text{CSLL}}. This choice corresponds to λ≈0.3\lambda\approx 0.3, for which 𝒪chiral\mathcal{O}_{\text{chiral}} is the most relevant perturbation when N≥4N\geq 4; see Table 3 and Appendix C. The final coupling we took is J⟂=0.28J_{\perp}=0.28, a compromise between analytical control (favoring small J⟂J_{\perp}) and numerical practicality (dictating larger J⟂J_{\perp}). At N=3N=3, 𝒪chiral\mathcal{O}_{\text{chiral}} stands in close competition with a magnetically ordered state but is favored by a parametrically larger bare coupling ∝J⟂\propto J_{\perp} versus J⟂2J_{\perp}^{2} for its competitor.

We numerically tested for the CSL signatures discussed in Sec. IV. For this purpose, we wrapped the lattice Hamiltonian around cylinders under different boundary conditions depicted in Fig. 2 and simulate this quasi-one-dimensional system with circumference N=3,4,5,6N=3,4,5,6 using finite-size DMRG and VUMPS achieved by the ITensor library [15, 14]. All simulations take advantage of the total SzS^{z} conservation and focus on the sectors with total Sz=0S^{z}=0 or 12\frac{1}{2}.

V.1 Spin pumping

We start to present numerical results from the spin-pumping property. For the descendant of the CSL in one dimension, a 2​π2\pi-flux insertion shifts the ground state to the other (degenerate) state with a different topological flux when the number of chain NN is sufficiently large, as discussed in Sec. IV. Simultaneously, the system transfers Sz=±1/2S^{z}=\pm 1/2 from the cylinder’s left end to the right end. The boundary spin value can be easily obtained from matrix product states (MPSs) describing finite systems. For an infinite MPS, we probe the boundary spin by looking at the spectrum of reduced density matrices of half-infinite cylinders [89]. The reduced density matrix ρL\rho_{L} of the left half-infinite cylinder is obtained by partially tracing out the sites with x>0x>0 from the density matrix |ψ⟩⟨ψ|\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}, where |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is the infinite MPS. Each eigenvector of ρL\rho_{L} corresponding to the eigenvalue pjp_{j} can also be a simultaneous eigenvector of ∑𝒓∈LS𝒓z\sum_{\bm{r}\in L}S^{z}_{\bm{r}} with eigenvalue SjzS^{z}_{j}. Thus, the left boundary spin is

SLz=∑jpj​Sjz.S^{z}_{L}=\sum_{j}p_{j}S^{z}_{j}\penalty\ . (37)

The correct spin-pumping features emerge in the three-chain systems. First, we find two degenerate ground states for the XC-3 cylinder with the same energy density (e=E/L≈−0.9985)(e=E/L\approx-0.9985) within numerical accuracy. The two states differ by whether there is a boundary spin 1/21/2 (ψs\psi_{s}) or not (ψ1\psi_{1}) for the left half-infinite system. To insert flux, we use the twisted boundary condition in the transverse direction and follow the adiabatic procedure of Refs. [29, 28, 27, 30, 74]. Specifically, we increase the flux Φ\Phi through the cylinder in small increments of π/10\pi/10, taking the state at the previous Φ\Phi as the initial state for the current iteration. Starting with the infinite MPS ψs\psi_{s} with boundary spin SLz=1/2S^{z}_{L}=1/2, we show the boundary spin of ψ⁡(Φ)\psi(\Phi) in Fig. 7(b). As anticipated, changing the flux by 2​π2\pi eliminates the boundary spin. Increasing the flux by another 2​π2\pi changes the boundary spin to SzL=−1/2S^{z}_{L}=-1/2.

Additionally, in Fig. 7(a), we monitor the fidelity per unit cell as a measure of how close the infinite MPS ψ⁡(Φ)\psi(\Phi) is to ψ1,s\psi_{1,s} in the bulk of the system [78]. A unit fidelity does not imply that two infinite MPSs are identical. In particular, the fidelity is insensitive to boundary effects, such as the residual spin, encoded in the MPSs. For further information about the fidelity, see Appendix D. As the twist angle increases, the fidelity between ψ⁡(Φ)\psi(\Phi) and ψs\psi_{s} decreases, i.e., the two states are orthogonal in the thermodynamic limit. After a 2​π2\pi flux insertion, the fidelity between ψ⁡(2​π)\psi(2\pi) and the second state, ψ1\psi_{1}, reaches unity. A second flux insertion recovers the original fidelity with ψs\psi_{s}.

In the case of N=5N=5 and N=6N=6, VUMPS did not converge for the chosen maximum bond dimension, which we attribute a large entanglement between neighboring unit cells representing adjacent rings on the cylinder. In this case, we observed a better-behaved convergence using finite-size cylinders, which we modeled using a finite MPS ansatz combined with DMRG. At N=5N=5, we choose an open XC-5 cylinder with L=31L=31 unit cells and focus on the ∑iSiz=1/2\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}=1/2 sector. Choosing an odd LL allows the system to have two degenerate ground states while the ground state is nondegenerate for an even and finite LL. For six-chain systems, we use the XC-6(0) boundary condition and pick L=32L=32. Similar to the three-chain case, we first prepare the state to have a spin of 1/21/2 at the left boundary, which corresponds to Φ=0\Phi=0 of Figs. 7(d) and 7(f). A 2​π2\pi-flux insertion eliminates the boundary spin, and the data across the flux insertion sit closely to the theoretical curve in blue.

In contrast, we do not find the same striking features for N=4N=4 cylinders. According to Table 2, the ground state is nondegenerate for four-chain systems. In practice, we find that the other supposedly degenerate state is embedded within the excited states, which impedes the flux insertion from swapping the two topological sectors. The same spin-pumping property should emerge once we make NN large enough, yet the next relevant value, N=8N=8, is still out of our simulation capacity. Consequently, we utilize other approaches to confirm the occurrence of the CSL in four-chain systems, as elaborated below.

V.2 Entanglement signatures

The entanglement spectrum of a CSL exhibits a universal pattern that can serve as a fingerprint [47]. Specifically, we consider the XC-N transverse boundary condition to maximize the allowed momentum values and introduce a real-space partition that separates the cylinder into two half-infinite subsystems. Due to the periodic boundary condition, the spectrum of the reduced density matrix for the left half-infinite system can be labeled by the transverse momentum ky∈{0,2​π/N,4​π/N,⋯,2​π​(1−1/N)}k_{y}\in\{0,2\pi/N,4\pi/N,\cdots,2\pi\left(1-1/N\right)\} in addition to the U(1) quantum number SzS^{z}. For the Kalmeyer-Laughlin CSL, this spectrum is expected to show several distinct features when NN is sufficiently large [54, 2]:

  1. 1.

    Lowest eigenvalue—The lowest eigenvalue is nondegenerate if the state is in the identity sector, while it is two-fold degenerate for states in the semion sector. In particular, the lowest eigenvalue occurs in two consecutive U⁡(1)U(1) quantum number sectors when it is doubly degenerate.

  2. 2.

    𝑼⁡(𝟏)\bm{U(1)} symmetry—The spectrum is symmetric around Sz=j0S^{z}=j_{0} for some j0j_{0}. Specifically, for every eigenvalue Ej​(ky)E_{j}(k_{y}), E2​j0−j​(ky)E_{2j_{0}-j}(k_{y}) is also an eigenvalue of the spectrum. Consequently, the lowest eigenvalue occurs in the Sz=j0S^{z}=j_{0} sector (identity) or the Sz=j0±1/2S^{z}=j_{0}\pm 1/2 sectors (semion).

  3. 3.

    Degeneracy pattern—The low-lying eigenvalue levels in each SzS^{z} sector correspond to one branch of chiral bosonic excitations governed by the U⁡(1)U(1) Kac-Moody algebra [84]. In particular, their degeneracies {1,1,2,3,5,7,11,⋯}\{1,1,2,3,5,7,11,\cdots\} are given by partitions of integers. Furthermore, the eigenvalue increases uniformly between consecutive momenta, quantized in units of 2​π/N2\pi/N 11 1 Without loss of generality, we pick δ​ky>0\delta k_{y}>0 by fixing a chirality.

  4. 4.

    Energy and momentum offsets—Up to a global shift and rescaling, the spacing between consecutive levels in each U⁡(1)U(1) quantum number sector is 11, and the lowest eigenvalue in the entire spectrum is 00 (1/41/4) for states in the identity (semion) sector. The momentum of the lowest level in the Sz=jS^{z}=j sector is

    k1(j)=k1(j0)+2​πN​(j−j0)2k_{1}^{(j)}=k_{1}^{(j_{0})}+\frac{2\pi}{N}\left(j-j_{0}\right)^{2} (38)

    for states in the identity sector and is

    k1(j)=k1(j0±1/2)+2​πN​[(j−j0)2−14]k_{1}^{(j)}=k_{1}^{(j_{0}\pm 1/2)}+\frac{2\pi}{N}\left[\left(j-j_{0}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\right] (39)

    for states in the semion sector.

Here, we show results from four- and five-chain cylinders. The VUMPS algorithm yields one state for four-chain systems under the XC-4 transverse boundary condition. As shown in Fig. 8, the lowest eigenvalue is doubly degenerate and occurs in Sz=−1,0S^{z}=-1,0 sectors, which means the state carries topological flux. It is further confirmed by the symmetric pattern shown in the spectrum. Moreover, the levels in each quantum number sector exhibit a clear chirality and follow the expected degeneracy pattern for a Laughlin state, i.e., 1,1,2,3,⋯1,1,2,3,\cdots [84, 54, 47].

We have observed similar properties of the entanglement spectra when N=5N=5. As mentioned in the previous subsection about spin pumping simulations, we utilize DMRG to simulate open cylinders with 3131 unit cells. Throughout the simulation, we cut the entire system so that the left half always has 1616 unit cells. Consequently, the MPS with a spin of 1/21/2 sitting at the left end should yield another spinon at the virtual boundary and, thus, is regarded as a state ψs\psi_{s} in the semion sector. Similarly, the other degenerate MPS ψ1\psi_{1} with a spin of 1/21/2 sitting at the right end corresponds to the identity sector. Figure 9 shows the momentum-resolved spectra of the two degenerate MPSs. The spectra are consistent with our assignment for the topological sector. Within each U⁡(1)U(1) quantum number sector, we have marked a few low-lying eigenvalues that obey the correct conformal field theory counting {1,1,2,3,5}\{1,1,2,3,5\}.

In six-chain cylinders, we find entanglement spectra whose counting is consistent with expectations but which are more strongly affected by the finite bond dimension or the system size. They are shown in Appendix E along with spectra for the three-chain system.

V.3 Quasi-one-dimensional signatures

To obtain additional evidence of CSL behavior, we use the other signatures derived in Sec. IV. Specifically, we argued that the topologically degenerate states reveal themselves by spontaneously breaking certain symmetries or by realizing SPT phases in quasi-one-dimension. In addition, the CSL precursors are characterized by specific non-local string order parameters.

According to Table 2, the system breaks xx-translation symmetry when the total number of chains NN is odd and 𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T} symmetry when N/2N/2 is odd. We tested for spontaneous symmetry breaking of translation symmetry by looking at the dimer operator

⟨𝒪Dimer​(𝒓+𝒃0/2)⟩≡⟨S→𝒓⋅S→𝒓+𝒃0⟩.\expectationvalue{\cO_{\text{Dimer}}(\bm{r}+\bm{b}_0/2)}\equiv\expectationvalue{\vec{S}_{\bm{r}} \cdot\vec{S}_{\bm{r} + \bm{b}_0}}\penalty\ . (40)

For a translationally invariant state along 𝒃0\bm{b}_{0}, this quantity is uniform; an oscillating ⟨𝒪Dimer⟩\expectationvalue{\cO_{\text{Dimer}}} thus implies a spontaneous symmetry breaking. The two expectation values in Fig. 10 relate to each other by the xx-translation in the bulk, which is consistent with the spontaneous symmetry breaking.

The spontaneous 𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T} symmetry breaking for XC-N(0) cylinders when N/2N/2 is odd manifests in the dimer operator in the transverse direction. Specifically, we define

𝒪𝒫​𝒯​(𝒓)≡S→𝒓⋅S→𝒓−𝒃+−S→𝒓⋅S→𝒓+𝒃−.\begin{split}\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}}(\bm{r})&\equiv\vec{S}_{\bm{r}}\cdot\vec{S}_{\bm{r}-\bm{b}_{+}}-\vec{S}_{\bm{r}}\cdot\vec{S}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{-}}\penalty\ .\end{split} (41)

This operator measures the difference of the two dimers and is odd under 𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}. Therefore, it must have zero expectation value for a 𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T} symmetric state. Nevertheless, the expectation value is non-zero in the bulk as shown in Fig. 10, indicating a spontaneous 𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T} symmetry breaking for both ψ1\psi_{1} and ψs\psi_{s}. We further note that the data also support 𝒫​𝒯​(ψ1)=ψs\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}(\psi_{1})=\psi_{s}, another signature of spontaneous symmetry breaking.

In four-chain (N=4N=4) systems, there is no spontaneous symmetry breaking according to Table 2. Indeed, we find a unique ground state ψs\psi_{s} being in the semion sector for the XC-4(0) cylinder using the VUMPS algorithm. When we consider a finite open cylinder, the corresponding ground state from DMRG shows spin 1/2 degrees of freedom at the boundaries (Fig. 11). Consequently, we suspect the symmetric ground state is adiabatically connected to the Haldane phase [24, 1]. To confirm our conjecture, we design an interpolation between our Hamiltonian on the XC-4(0) cylinder and

HHaldane=∑j(S→j−12,1+S→j−12,3)⋅(S→j,2+S→j,4)+∑j(S→j,2+S→j,4)⋅(S→j+12,1+S→j+12,3),\begin{split}H_{\text{Haldane}}&=\sum_{j}\left(\vec{S}_{j-\frac{1}{2},1}+\vec{S}_{j-\frac{1}{2},3}\right)\cdot\left(\vec{S}_{j,2}+\vec{S}_{j,4}\right)\\ &+\sum_{j}\left(\vec{S}_{j,2}+\vec{S}_{j,4}\right)\cdot\left(\vec{S}_{j+\frac{1}{2},1}+\vec{S}_{j+\frac{1}{2},3}\right)\penalty\ ,\end{split} (42)

which can be viewed as a two-leg spin ladder (see the inset in Fig. 11). The model has been shown to lie in the Haldane phase in Refs. [72, 41]. The linear interpolation preserves all the symmetries in our model because they are also symmetries in HHaldaneH_{\text{Haldane}}. The correlation lengths of the infinite MPSs during the interpolation are shown in Fig. 11. The solid dots are data obtained from infinite MPSs at different bond dimensions, and the lines connect the data from the largest bond dimension. Since the correlation length does not diverge, we conclude that the two phases are adiabatically connected.

Finally, we examine different string operators on infinite three- and four-chain cylinders. For three-chain cylinders, there are three different types of strings, namely the single string s1β​(x)s_{1}^{\beta}(x), a product of two strings ∏y=12syβ​(x)\prod_{y=1}^{2}s_{y}^{\beta}(x), and the full string ∏y=13syβ​(x)\prod_{y=1}^{3}s_{y}^{\beta}(x). Using the two different ground states with or without a topological flux, we find that only the full string develops a nonzero expectation value. The other two strings decay exponentially when the length of the strings increases (Fig. 12). The same behavior can also be found using the infinite MPS of the XC-4(0) four-chain cylinder (Fig. 13).

V.4 Two-dimensional results

To supplement the investigation on cylinders of finite circumference illustrated in the previous sections, we employ iPEPS [79, 35] to study the behavior of the model described in Secs. II and III in the two-dimensional thermodynamic limit. The iPEPS is a subclass of tensor network states defined directly on infinite two-dimensional lattices. They fulfill by construction an area law of entanglement entropy and are thus well suited to the study of ground states of local Hamiltonians in two spatial dimensions. We note that, by contrast, one-dimensional ansätze like MPS do not fulfill the area law in two dimensions. Hence, if applied to pseudo-two-dimensional geometries like finite-circumference cylinders, one needs to use bond dimensions that are exponentially large in the cylinder circumference. Once equipped with state-of-the-art variational optimization [12, 48, 58, 57], the utility of the iPEPS ansatz for the numerical study of chiral topological states has recently been demonstrated both in the case of spin systems [26] as well as in the study of mobile bosons in a static gauge field [81].

Generically, the correlations of the system require an iPEPS ansatz consisting of an alternation between two independent local tensors on even and odd rungs of the model. The local tensors within one rung can be chosen to be identical. To be able to use a fully translation-invariant iPEPS ansatz, we perform a sub-lattice rotation Usub=∏ji​σjyU_{\text{sub}}=\prod_{j}i\sigma^{y}_{j}, where the product runs over all lattice sites on even rungs of the system. We can use this ansatz since the Hamiltonian has a U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry we can utilize [25]. We illustrate this ansatz in Fig. 14. With this ansatz, we find ground states for several bond dimensions dd, whose energy density ee and local magnetization m2m^{2} we list in Table 4, and we further analyze the states via their entanglement spectrum below. We want to note that we found in the iPEPS simulation a competing ground state that breaks the sublattice structure and needs a CDDC\begin{smallmatrix}C&D\\ D&C\end{smallmatrix} unit cell with two independent tensors CC and DD. For the maximal available bond dimension up to d=7d=7, this state is slightly lower in energy. With available data, we could not resolve if this is an effect of the finite bond dimension and the additional restriction due to the sublattice ansatz. But a extrapolation of the energy difference between both states as shown in Fig. 15 (left/blue yy axis) suggests that the states will coincide in the limit of larger dimensions. Additionally, the magnetization of the CDDC\begin{smallmatrix}C&D\\ D&C\end{smallmatrix} state seems to vanish in the extrapolation to large bond dimensions as well as shown in Fig. 15 (right/red yy axis).

Once we have obtained an approximation of the ground state in terms of an iPEPS wavefunction, we can access information about its edge spectrum by employing the PEPS bulk-boundary correspondence [10]. This allows us to compute the entanglement spectrum of a bipartition of the system, which, following Li and Haldane [47], is related to the low-lying physical spectrum on the edge. To observe the degeneracy counting of the chiral entanglement spectrum, we are setting our system on a finite cylinder to discretize the momenta. We show the entanglement spectrum obtained on a circumference-eight cylinder in Fig. 16. We can clearly identify a chiral spectrum and the degeneracy counting of the partition of integers associated with the edge spectrum of the Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin liquid.

VI Discussion

In this article, we have demonstrated how to obtain a microscopic lattice Hamiltonian of the Kalmeyer-Laughlin CSL from a coupled-wire construction. The crucial step lies in introducing nonperturbative intrawire interactions to realize a gapless fixed point (sliding Luttinger liquid, SLL) whose strongest instability is toward the CSL. We constructed these couplings with the help of a duality that allowed us analytical control over the parameters of the SLL.

By using extensive numerical simulations of quasi-one-dimensional systems with DMRG and VUMPS and in two dimensions via iPEPS, we confirmed that the lattice model realizes a CSL ground state. The connection between the lattice models and coupled-wire analysis allowed us to make sharp numerical predictions about the CSL beyond spectral flow and entanglement spectra. In particular, we showed that infinite cylinders of different circumferences NN follow a specific sequence of quasi-one-dimensional phases. Additionally, we introduced nonlocal operators that serve as order parameters for numerical simulations.

The lattice models that we study include multispin interactions, which are sometimes regarded as unnatural. However, we note that all the interactions in our models arise in the t/Ut/U expansion of a generalized Hubbard model with the appropriate symmetries [51, 19, 52]. Consequently, one may expect such Hamiltonians to arise for “weak” Mott insulators, where virtual charge fluctuations are significant. Unfortunately, the precise relation between couplings used in this study is not achievable in a nearest-neighbor model with purely on-site repulsion. Still, longer-range hoppings or interactions could improve this situation and better approximate the spin models we investigated here. Alternatively, quantum simulators may be able to directly engineer the spin-spin interactions.

This work demonstrates a prescription to turn coupled-wire constructions from analytical toy models to concrete microscopic systems. All the analytical and numerical steps in our analysis can be adapted for known coupled-wire constructions of other spin liquids and fractional quantum Hall or Chern insulators [39, 75, 63, 32, 31, 44, 7, 45, 46, 70]. In particular, the duality relation used to construct suitable SLL fixed points readily generalizes to those contexts: the operator SzS^{z} in Eq. (12) is replaced by the particle number in itinerant models.

For more exotic topological states, coupled wire constructions use multichannel Luttinger liquids as a starting point. Reference [75] constructed wire models of S​U​(2)nSU(2)_{n} topological orders based on nn-channel Luttinger liquids. In those cases, the single analytically controlled parameter α\alpha in the SLL of Eq. 15 can be replaced by n2n^{2} parameters ασ,σ′\alpha_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}. The corresponding lattice model can be obtained by reversing the analysis of Sec. III with a generalized duality transformation. Specifically, Eq. (20) can be generalized to dress S𝒓,σ−S^{-}_{\bm{r},\sigma} with independent string operators for each channel σ′\sigma^{\prime} on the neighboring wires. We expect that this level of analytical control over the long-wavelength properties of a lattice model will permit the realization of more exotic topological phases, including non-Abelian states.

Numerical studies of spin-1 and spin-3/2 on the triangular lattice showed evidence of CSLs with non-Abelian S​U​(2)2SU(2)_{2} and S​U​(2)3SU(2)_{3} order, respectively [33, 50]. Together with the Kalmeyer-Laughlin CSL in spin-1/2 system, these findings suggest a pattern of S​U​(2)2​S+1SU(2)_{2S+1} spin liquids for spin SS. Comparison with the coupled-wire construction mentioned in the previous paragraph implies that this spin corresponds to n=2​S+1n=2S+1 channels. To understand this relation, we note that spin SS models can generally realize an S​U​(2​S+1)1SU(2S+1)_{1} Wess-Zumino-Witten [85, 88] conformal field theory, which has central charge c=2​S+1c=2S+1. (For example, the biquadratic spin-1 chain at the Uimin-Lai-Sutherland point realizes the S​U​(3)1SU(3)_{1} theory [77, 42, 73, 34].) We expect that spin SS chains realizing these critical points would be suitable building blocks for constructing lattice models of S​U​(2)2​S+1SU(2)_{2S+1} CSL.

Appendix A Duality transformation

In Eq. (20), we introduced a transformation from Sx,y,zS^{x,y,z} to new variables S~x,y,z\tilde{S}^{x,y,z} that preserves their commutation relations. We then argued that Eq. (24) is the corresponding transformation from the field theory variables θ,φ\theta,\varphi to θ~,φ~\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\varphi}. Here, we provide a detailed derivation and numerical support.

A.1 String operators

The central element of this mapping is the string operator

σx,x+n≡2​∑m=0nS𝒓+m​𝒃0z=2​∑m=0nS~𝒓+m​𝒃0z,\displaystyle\sigma_{x,x+n}\equiv 2\sum_{m=0}^{n}S^{z}_{\bm{r}+m\bm{b}_{0}}=2\sum_{m=0}^{n}\tilde{S}^{z}_{\bm{r}+m\bm{b}_{0}}\penalty\ , (43)

which is a sum of commuting terms that each square to unity. We are suppressing the wire index yy when there is no danger of ambiguity to lighten the notation. The string operator enters the lattice duality transformation through

sx,x+nα≡∏j=0nR𝒓+j​𝒃0α=exp⁡(−i​α​π2​σx,x+n),s^{\alpha}_{x,x+n}\equiv\prod_{j=0}^{n}R^{\alpha}_{\bm{r}+j\bm{b}_{0}}=\exp{-i \alpha\frac{\pi}{2} \sigma_{x,x+n}}\penalty\ , (44)

which satisfies the periodic property

sx,x+nα+2=(−1)n+1​sx,x+nα.\displaystyle s^{\alpha+2}_{x,x+n}=(-1)^{n+1}s^{\alpha}_{x,x+n}\penalty\ . (45)

To obtain expressions of σ\sigma and ss in terms of θ,φ\theta,\varphi, we use Eq. (6a) in Eq. (43) and drop the oscillatory term to obtain

σx,x+n≈2π​[θ⁡(x+n)−θ⁡(x)]=2π​[θ~​(x+n)−θ~​(x)].\displaystyle\sigma_{x,x+n}\approx\frac{2}{\pi}\left[\theta(x+n)-\theta(x)\right]=\frac{2}{\pi}\left[\tilde{\theta}(x+n)-\tilde{\theta}(x)\right]. (46)

Inserting this relation into Eq. (44) yields

sx,x+nα≈ei​α​[θ⁡(x+n)−θ⁡(x)],\displaystyle s^{\alpha}_{x,x+n}\approx e^{i\alpha[\theta(x+n)-\theta(x)]}\penalty\ , (47)

which does not satisfy Eq. (45). To enforce the periodic property, one could instead take

sx,x+nα∼∑kr0(k)​ei⁡(α+4​k)​[θ⁡(x+n)−θ⁡(x)]+(−1)n∑krπ(k)e−i⁡(2−α+4​k)​[θ⁡(x+n)−θ⁡(x)].\begin{split}s^{\alpha}_{x,x+n}&\sim\sum_{k}r_{0}^{(k)}e^{i\left(\alpha+4k\right)\left[\theta\left(x+n\right)-\theta(x)\right]}\\ &+(-1)^{n}\sum_{k}r_{\pi}^{(k)}e^{-i\left(2-\alpha+4k\right)\left[\theta\left(x+n\right)-\theta(x)\right]}\penalty\ .\end{split} (48)

However, unless α\alpha is an odd integer, there is a single component on the sum on the right-hand side that dominates at large nn. In particular, for α∈(−1,1)\alpha\in(-1,1), the dominant contribution is the one in Eq. (47).

In a single chain with Luttinger parameter KK, we find

⟨sx,x+nα⟩∼r0n−α2K/2+rπ(−1)nn−(2−α)2K/2+⋯,\displaystyle\expectationvalue{s^{\alpha}_{x,x+n}}\sim r_{0}n^{-\alpha^{2}K/2}+r_{\pi}(-1)^{n}n^{-(2-\alpha)^{2}K/2}+\cdots\penalty\ , (49)

In Fig. 17, we show numerical data obtained from a single X​X​ZXXZ chain using VUMPS up to bond dimension 100100. Both the uniform and the staggered parts of the expectation value follow the expected power laws.

A.2 Transformations on the field variables

Since the spin zz components are untouched during the nonlocal transformation Eq. (20), the fields θy\theta_{y} and θ~y\tilde{\theta}_{y} are identical, i.e., θy=θ~y\theta_{y}=\tilde{\theta}_{y}. To infer how φy\varphi_{y} is related to the dual variables, we note that the dual spin operators S~𝒓−\tilde{S}^{-}_{\bm{r}} are defined in Eq. (20) as

S~𝒓−=S𝒓−⋅s−∞,𝒓−𝒃−α⋅s𝒓+𝒃−,+∞α.\displaystyle\tilde{S}^{-}_{\bm{r}}=S^{-}_{\bm{r}}\cdot s^{\alpha}_{-\infty,\bm{r}-\bm{b}_{-}}\cdot s^{\alpha}_{\bm{r}+\bm{b}_{-},+\infty}\penalty\ . (50)

Using Eq. (47) and dropping terms at infinities, we find

S~x,y−≈Sx,y−⋅ei​α​θy−1​(x)⋅e−i​α​θy+1​(x).\displaystyle\tilde{S}^{-}_{x,y}\approx{S}^{-}_{x,y}\cdot e^{i\alpha\theta_{y-1}(x)}\cdot e^{-i\alpha\theta_{y+1}(x)}\penalty\ . (51)

Since S~−∝ei​φ~\tilde{S}^{-}\propto e^{i\tilde{\varphi}} and S−∝ei​φS^{-}\propto e^{i\varphi}, we conclude that φy≡φ~y−α​θ~y−1+α​θ~y+1\varphi_{y}\equiv\tilde{\varphi}_{y}-\alpha\tilde{\theta}_{y-1}+\alpha\tilde{\theta}_{y+1}.

A.3 Numerical tests of the duality

We tested the validity of Eq. (15) on a two-leg ladder by numerically computing thermodynamic quantities that are fully determined by the field theory parameters u,K,αu,K,\alpha. Specifically, we used periodic boundary conditions along xx with opposite twist ±Φ\pm\Phi for the two chains and open boundaries in the yy direction. The lattice Hamiltonian for this system is the same as what was studied in Ref. [65]. In this case, the field-theoretic duality mapping reduces to φ1=φ~1+α​θ~2\varphi_{1}=\tilde{\varphi}_{1}+\alpha\tilde{\theta}_{2} and φ2=φ~2−α​θ~1\varphi_{2}=\tilde{\varphi}_{2}-\alpha\tilde{\theta}_{1}. We thus obtain the long-wavelength Hamiltonian density

ℋ=u2​π​∑y=12[(1K+α2​K)​(∇θy)2+K​(∇φy)2]+u​Kπ​α​[(∇φ1)​(∇θ2)−(∇φ2)​(∇θ1)].\begin{split}\mathcal{H}&=\frac{u}{2\pi}\sum_{y=1}^{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{K}+\alpha^{2}K\right)\left(\gradient\theta_{y}\right)^{2}+K\left(\gradient\varphi_{y}\right)^{2}\right]\\ &+\frac{uK}{\pi}\alpha\left[\left(\gradient\varphi_{1}\right)\left(\gradient\theta_{2}\right)-\left(\gradient\varphi_{2}\right)\left(\gradient\theta_{1}\right)\right].\end{split} (52)

It is straightforward to compute the ground-state energy EE of the quadratic theory as a function of the twist Φ\Phi, system size LL, and the total spin N≡−1π∫x(∂xθ1+∂xθ2)N\equiv-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{x}\,\left(\partial_{x}\theta_{1}+\partial_{x}\theta_{2}\right). In particular, we find the derivatives evaluated at Φ=N=0\Phi=N=0 to be

L​∂2E∂N2=π2​(uK+α2​u​K),L​∂2E∂Φ2=2π​u​K,L​∂2E∂N​∂Φ=u​K​α.\begin{split}L\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial N^{2}}&=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{u}{K}+\alpha^{2}uK\right)\penalty\ ,\\ L\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial\Phi^{2}}&=\frac{2}{\pi}uK\penalty\ ,\\ L\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial N\partial\Phi}&=uK\alpha\penalty\ .\end{split} (53)

Our numerical DMRG simulations on a 2×322\times 32 system are shown in Fig. 18 and demonstrate excellent agreement with the analytical prediction.

A.4 Duality near odd integer α\alpha

When deriving the duality transformation of the long-wavelength variables, we kept only the leading term in Eq. (48). By comparing the two terms in Eq. (49), we estimate a length scale ℓ\ell beyond which this approximation is valid. Specifically, we require that

ϵ≡ℓ−(2−α)2​K2ℓ−α2​K2≪1.\displaystyle\epsilon\equiv\frac{\ell^{-(2-\alpha)^{2}\frac{K}{2}}}{\ell^{-\alpha^{2}\frac{K}{2}}}\ll 1\penalty\ . (54)

As α→1\alpha\rightarrow 1, the length scale ℓ\ell diverges, and there is no parametric regime where dropping the subleading term would be justified.

We note that α→±1\alpha\rightarrow\pm 1 yield the same microscopic models, but the scaling dimensions of 𝒪chiral{\cal O}_{\text{chiral}}, according to Eq. (16), differ significantly in the two limits. Reassuringly, the time reversed partner of Eq. (18), i.e.,

𝒪chiral′=cos⁡((2​θy−1+2​θy+2+φy−φy+1)),{\cal O}^{\prime}_{\text{chiral}}=\cos{\left(2\theta_{y-1} + 2\theta_{y+2} + \varphi_y - \varphi_{y+1}\right)}\penalty\ , (55)

which realizes the same topological phase as 𝒪chiral{\cal O}_{\text{chiral}} has a scaling dimension that satisfies Δantichiral|−2−α=Δchiral′|α\Delta_{\text{antichiral}}\big|_{-2-\alpha}=\Delta_{\text{chiral}}^{\prime}\big|_{\alpha}.

Appendix C Scaling dimensions

The SLL fixed point in Eq. (15), together with all symmetry-allowed perturbations, captures the low-energy physics of our lattice model as long as the interwire couplings J⟂zJ^{z}_{\perp} and J⟂J_{\perp} are sufficiently small. When the perturbation 𝒪chiral\mathcal{O}_{\text{chiral}} has the smallest scaling dimension, the system will flow to the CSL phase. To quantify this statement, we deduce the scaling dimensions of

𝒪chiral\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\text{chiral}} =cos⁡((2​θy+2​θy+1+φy−φy+1)),\displaystyle=\cos{\left(2\theta_y + 2\theta_{y+1} + \varphi_y - \varphi_{y+1}\right)}\penalty\ ,
𝒪antichiral′\displaystyle{\cal O}^{\prime}_{\text{antichiral}} =cos⁡((2​θy−1+2​θy+2−φy+φy+1)),\displaystyle=\cos{\left(2\theta_{y-1} + 2\theta_{y+2} - \varphi_y + \varphi_{y+1}\right)}\penalty\ ,
𝒪X​Y\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{XY} =cos⁡((φy−φy+2)),\displaystyle=\cos{\left(\varphi_y - \varphi_{y+2}\right)}\penalty\ ,
𝒪spiral\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\text{spiral}} =(∇φy+∇φy+1)​sin⁡((φy−φy+1)),\displaystyle=\left(\gradient\varphi_{y}+\gradient\varphi_{y+1}\right)\sin{\left(\varphi_y - \varphi_{y+1}\right)}\penalty\ ,
𝒪θ±\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\pm}_{\theta} =cos⁡((2​θy±2​θy+2)).\displaystyle=\cos{\left(2\theta_y \pm 2\theta_{y+2}\right)}\penalty\ . (63)

When the operators 𝒪θ+\mathcal{O}^{+}_{\theta} and 𝒪θ−\mathcal{O}^{-}_{\theta} flow to strong coupling, they give the same effect as 𝒪VBS\mathcal{O}_{\text{VBS}} or 𝒪Ising\mathcal{O}_{\text{Ising}}, depending on how the arguments are pinned to extrema. Besides, 𝒪antichiral′{\cal O}^{\prime}_{\text{antichiral}} defined here can also lead to the CSL with an opposite chirality similar to 𝒪antichiral{\cal O}_{\text{antichiral}} in the main text, whose scaling dimension is generally larger at a nonzero positive α\alpha.

We obtain the scaling dimensions using the dual formulation in terms of the field variables φ~y\tilde{\varphi}_{y} and θ~y′\tilde{\theta}_{y^{\prime}}. Correlation functions involving φ~y\tilde{\varphi}_{y} and θ~y′\tilde{\theta}_{y^{\prime}} take relatively simple forms at the SLL of Eq. (15). The fixed point is translationally invariant in the transverse direction; therefore, we introduce Fourier modes for the fields as

φ~y=1N​∑qei​q​y​φ~q,θ~y=1N​∑qei​q​y​θ~q.\tilde{\varphi}_{y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{q}e^{iqy}\tilde{\varphi}_{q},\qquad\tilde{\theta}_{y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{q}e^{iqy}\tilde{\theta}_{q}. (64)

Using these new variables, we rewrite Eq. (15) as

ℋCSLL=u2​π​∑q(1+2​λ​cos⁡(q)K​|∂xθ~q|2+K​|∂xφ~q|2).\mathcal{H}_{\text{CSLL}}=\frac{u}{2\pi}\sum_{q}\left(\frac{1+2\lambda\cos{q}}{K}|\partial_{x}\tilde{\theta}_{q}|^{2}+K|\partial_{x}\tilde{\varphi}_{q}|^{2}\right)\penalty\ . (65)

Modes at different momentum qq decouple. For each momentum qq, the effective Luttinger parameter is

Kq​(λ)=K1+2​λ​cos⁡(q).\displaystyle K_{q}(\lambda)=\frac{K}{\sqrt{1+2\lambda\cos{q}}}\penalty\ . (66)

We conclude that the field correlation functions are

⟨|θ~q​(r)−θ~q​(0)|2⟩\displaystyle\expectationvalue{|\Tilde{\theta}_q(r) - \Tilde{\theta}_q(0)|^2} ∼Kq​(λ)​log⁡(|r|),\displaystyle\sim K_{q}(\lambda)\log{|r|}\penalty\ , (67)
⟨|φ~q​(r)−φ~q​(0)|2⟩\displaystyle\expectationvalue{|\Tilde{\varphi}_q(r) - \Tilde{\varphi}_q(0)|^2} ∼log⁡(|r|)Kq​(λ).\displaystyle\sim\frac{\log{|r|}}{K_{q}(\lambda)}\penalty\ . (68)

Correlation functions such as ⟨θ~y​(r)​θ~y′​(0)⟩\expectationvalue{\Tilde{\theta}_y(r) \Tilde{\theta}_{y'}(0)} can be expressed using these correlators. We find

⟨θ~y​(r)​θ~y+n​(0)⟩=1N​∑qKq​(λ)​cos⁡((n​q))​log⁡(|r|).\begin{split}\expectationvalue{\Tilde{\theta}_y(r) \Tilde{\theta}_{y+n}(0)}&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{q}K_{q}(\lambda)\cos{\left(nq\right)}\log{|r|}\penalty\ .\end{split} (69)

In the two-dimensional limit where N→∞N\rightarrow\infty, the summation becomes an integral, and we can rewrite it as

⟨θ~y​(r)​θ~y+n​(0)⟩=log⁡(|r|)​K2​π​∫02​πd​φ​cos⁡((n​φ))1+2​λ​cos⁡(φ)≡K​fn−​(λ)​log⁡(|r|),\begin{split}\expectationvalue{\Tilde{\theta}_y(r) \Tilde{\theta}_{y+n}(0)}&=\log{|r|}\frac{K}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\mathrm{d}\varphi\,\frac{\cos{\left(n\varphi\right)}}{\sqrt{1+2\lambda\cos{\varphi}}}\\ &\equiv Kf^{-}_{n}(\lambda)\log{|r|}\penalty\ ,\end{split} (70)

where we introduced

fn±​(λ)=12​π​∫02​πd​φ​cos⁡((n​φ))​(1+2​λ​cos⁡(φ))±12f^{\pm}_{n}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\mathrm{d}\varphi\,\cos{\left(n\varphi\right)}\left(1+2\lambda\cos{\varphi}\right)^{\pm\frac{1}{2}} (71)

to lighten equations. Similarly, the expression for the other field operator correlation function ⟨φ~y​(r)​φ~y′​(0)⟩\expectationvalue{\Tilde{\varphi}_y(r) \Tilde{\varphi}_{y'}(0)} is

⟨φ~y​(r)​φ~y′​(0)⟩=1N​∑q1Kq​(λ)​cos⁡((n​q))​log⁡(|r|)→N→∞log⁡(|r|)K​fn+​(λ).\begin{split}\expectationvalue{\Tilde{\varphi}_y(r) \Tilde{\varphi}_{y'}(0)}&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{q}\frac{1}{K_{q}(\lambda)}\cos{\left(nq\right)}\log{|r|}\\ &\xrightarrow{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\log{|r|}}{K}f^{+}_{n}(\lambda)\penalty\ .\end{split} (72)

Since cos⁡((φ))\cos{(\varphi)} is bounded between −1-1 and 11, we can expand fn±​(λ)f^{\pm}_{n}(\lambda) as a power series when λ<1\lambda<1, i.e.,

f2​k±​(λ)=∑m=k∞λ2​m​(±122​m)​(2​m)!(m−k)!​(m+k)!,f2​k+1±​(λ)=∑m=k∞λ2​m+1​(±122​m+1)​(2​m+1)!(m−k)!​(m+k+1)!.\begin{split}f^{\pm}_{2k}(\lambda)&=\sum_{m=k}^{\infty}\lambda^{2m}\binom{\pm\frac{1}{2}}{2m}\frac{(2m)!}{(m-k)!(m+k)!}\penalty\ ,\\ f^{\pm}_{2k+1}(\lambda)&=\sum_{m=k}^{\infty}\lambda^{2m+1}\binom{\pm\frac{1}{2}}{2m+1}\frac{(2m+1)!}{(m-k)!(m+k+1)!}\penalty\ .\end{split} (73)

In particular, fn±​(λ)=O⁡(λn)f_{n}^{\pm}(\lambda)=O(\lambda^{n}) and f0f_{0} do not receive corrections at the first order in λ\lambda.

All scaling dimensions in the two-dimensional limit (N→∞N\rightarrow\infty) can be expressed as a linear combination of fn±​(λ)f^{\pm}_{n}(\lambda) and thus inherit a power series expansion from Eq. (73). One needs, at most, six field operator correlation functions to get the correlation function of the CSL operator 𝒪chiral\mathcal{O}_{\text{chiral}}. From its correlation function, we obtain its scaling dimension as

Δchiral=K⁡[(2−α)2+α22​f0−​(λ)+4−α22​f1−​(λ)]+K⁡[(2−α)​α​f2−​(λ)+α22​f3−​(λ)]+12​K​[f0+​(λ)−f1+​(λ)].\begin{split}\Delta_{\text{chiral}}&=K\left[\frac{(2-\alpha)^{2}+\alpha^{2}}{2}f_{0}^{-}(\lambda)+\frac{4-\alpha^{2}}{2}f_{1}^{-}(\lambda)\right]\\ &+K\left[\left(2-\alpha\right)\alpha f_{2}^{-}(\lambda)+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}f_{3}^{-}(\lambda)\right]\\ &+\frac{1}{2K}\left[f_{0}^{+}(\lambda)-f_{1}^{+}(\lambda)\right].\end{split} (74)

The other scaling dimensions can be obtained in the same manner. The operator leading to the CSL with an opposite chirality has a scaling dimension Δantichiral′​(α)=Δchiral​(2−α)\Delta^{\prime}_{\text{antichiral}}(\alpha)=\Delta_{\text{chiral}}(2-\alpha). The results for the other four operators are

Δθ±=2​K​[f0−​(λ)±f2−​(λ)],\displaystyle\Delta_{\theta}^{\pm}=2K\left[f_{0}^{-}(\lambda)\pm f_{2}^{-}(\lambda)\right]\penalty\ , (75)
Δspiral=1+12​K​[f0+​(λ)−f1+​(λ)]\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{spiral}}=1+\frac{1}{2K}\left[f_{0}^{+}(\lambda)-f_{1}^{+}(\lambda)\right]
+K⁡[α2​f0−​(λ)−α22​f1−​(λ)−α2​f2−​(λ)+α22​f3−​(λ)],\displaystyle+K\left[\alpha^{2}f_{0}^{-}(\lambda)-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}f_{1}^{-}(\lambda)-\alpha^{2}f_{2}^{-}(\lambda)+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}f_{3}^{-}(\lambda)\right]\penalty\ , (76)
ΔX​Y=K⁡[32​α2​f0−​(λ)−2​α2​f2−​(λ)+α22​f4−​(λ)]\displaystyle\Delta_{XY}=K\left[\frac{3}{2}\alpha^{2}f_{0}^{-}(\lambda)-2\alpha^{2}f_{2}^{-}(\lambda)+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}f_{4}^{-}(\lambda)\right]
+12​K​[f0+​(λ)−f2+​(λ)].\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2K}\left[f_{0}^{+}(\lambda)-f_{2}^{+}(\lambda)\right]\penalty\ . (77)

These dimensions are plotted for J∥z=−0.1J^{z}_{\parallel}=-0.1 and α=0.75\alpha=0.75 as functions of λ\lambda in Fig. 6. The figure also contains several plots for quasi-one-dimensional cylinders with finite NN, for which Eq. (69) must be evaluated as a sum. We do not provide an explicit formula for arbitrary NN, but the computation for any particular choice contains a finite number of terms and is thus straightforward.

Generalizations to multisite systems can be found, for example, in Ref. [90].

The dominant contribution to an inner product of two infinite MPS is encoded in the (mixed) transfer matrix. The overlap ⟨Ψ⁡(A)|Ψ⁡(B)⟩\innerproduct{\Psi(A)}{\Psi(B)} involves contractions of the mixed transfer matrix

\hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}} (79)

to an infinite number of times. A properly normalized infinite MPS |Ψ⁡(A)⟩\ket{\Psi(A)}, thus, should have 11 as the largest eigenvalue of T⁡(A,A)T(A,A).

Another measure of the similarity between two infinite MPSs is the fidelity per site, which we have mentioned in Sec V. Since the inner product between two infinite MPSs involves an infinite product of the mixed transfer matrix, even locally very similar states can be orthogonal to each other in the thermodynamic limit, given that the largest eigenvalue of T⁡(A,B)T(A,B) is less than 11. Consequently, it is conventional to use the number instead, also named as the fidelity per site, to quantify how similar the two states are in the bulk of a system, i.e.,

f⁡(A,B)=maxT⁡(A,B)​v=λ​v⁡|λ|.f(A,B)=\max_{T(A,B)v=\lambda v}|\lambda|\penalty\ . (80)

Finally, the transfer matrix T⁡(A,A)T(A,A) can also reveal the correlation length of an infinite MPS |Ψ⁡(A)⟩\ket{\Psi(A)}. In our normalization scheme, the spectrum of the transfer matrix associated with a generic infinite MPS always has 11 as the unique dominant eigenvalue [78]. The second largest eigenvalue then determines the long-distance behaviors of the system. Consequently, the correlation length is

ξ≡maxλ≠1⁡−1ln⁡(|λ|).\xi\equiv\max_{\lambda\neq 1}\frac{-1}{\ln{|\lambda|}}\penalty\ . (81)

Appendix E Additional numerical data

In the main text, we have shown extensive numerical evidence in support of the CSL. Here, we provide additional data showing correlation lengths, entanglement spectra, and dependence on the bond dimension.

E.1 Many-body energy gap and magnetic orders

Since we consider a periodic boundary condition in the transverse direction, the cylinder must have a gapped spectrum if we realize the CSL. We probe the gap indirectly by examining the correlation length and the central charge. For the three-chain cylinder, we obtain the correlation length at each bond dimension χ∈{200,300,⋯,2000}\chi\in\{200,300,\cdots,2000\} for both infinite MPSs ψ1\psi_{1} and ψs\psi_{s} [Fig. 20(a)]. Extrapolations of the correlation length yield finite values as χ→∞\chi\rightarrow\infty, which is compatible with a many-body gap in the system. We further confirm this conjecture by examining the scaling behavior of the entanglement entropy against ln⁡((ξ))\ln{\left(\xi\right)} in Fig. 20(b). For a gapless one-dimensional system, its entanglement entropy scales as

S=c6​ln⁡((ξ))+S0,S=\frac{c}{6}\ln{\left(\xi\right)}+S_{0}\penalty\ , (82)

where c≠0c\neq 0 is the central charge, and S0S_{0} is a nonuniversal constant [5]. The entanglement entropy data in Fig. 20(b) bend flat as ln⁡((ξ))\ln{\left(\xi\right)} increases, indicating the central charge is 00. Similar to the N=3N=3 case, the ground state for four-chain cylinders under the XC-4(0) boundary condition also has a finite correlation length and a zero central charge [Figs. 20(c) and 20(d)].

We then use the states to examine spin operator correlation functions. The four small panels in Fig. 21 show correlation functions calculated by the wave function ψs\psi_{s} at χ=2000\chi=2000 for the three-chain cylinder. The correlation in the spin X​YXY plane shows perfect exponential decay, which is in agreement with the formation of descendants of the CSL. The other two panels have data affected more significantly by numerical errors. Still, the data follow modestly exponential decaying laws. The larger panel at the bottom shows the correlation functions for the XC-4(0) cylinder at χ=1000\chi=1000. All of the functions decay exponentially, which means the ground state does not have any magnetic order.

E.2 Spontaneous symmetry breaking for N=3N=3

Based on Table 2, three-chain cylinders should also break the translation symmetry as N=5N=5 systems. We thus simulate the model with a six-site VUMPS ansatz to accommodate Sz=0S^{z}=0 and permit translation-symmetry breaking. We have observed that the expectation value of 𝒪Dimer\mathcal{O}_{\text{Dimer}} defined in Eq. (40) exhibits relatively small oscillating behavior. Therefore, to single out the oscillating part, we consider

⟨𝒪~Dimer​(x,y)⟩=limL→∞1L​∑x′(−1)x′−x​⟨S→x′,y⋅S→x′+1,y⟩=12​⟨S→x,y⋅S→x+1,y⟩−12​⟨S→x+1,y⋅S→x+2,y⟩.\begin{split}\expectationvalue{\Tilde{\mathcal{O}}_\text{Dimer}(x,y)}&=\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{L}\sum_{x^{\prime}}(-1)^{x^{\prime}-x}\expectationvalue{\vec{S}_{x',y} \cdot\vec{S}_{x' + 1,y}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\expectationvalue{\vec{S}_{x,y} \cdot\vec{S}_{x+1,y}}-\frac{1}{2}\expectationvalue{\vec{S}_{x+1,y} \cdot\vec{S}_{x+2,y}}.\end{split} (83)

The second equality holds since the wave function is an infinite uniform MPS, and it will serve as our way to obtain ⟨𝒪~Dimer⟩\expectationvalue{\Tilde{\mathcal{O}}_\text{Dimer}}. Figure 22 shows this quantity for the two states ψ1,s\psi_{1,s} at different bond dimensions. The quantity saturates at a nonzero value for both states, indicating a spontaneously broken translation symmetry.

E.3 Entanglement spectra data for N=3,6N=3,6

The main text only contains entanglement spectra for four- and five-chain cylinders. We have also observed similar results for N=6N=6 (see Fig. 23), yet the quality is not as superior as Figs. 8 and 9. In particular, we observed that the momentum of the lowest eigenvalue in the Sz=−2S^{z}=-2 and Sz=1S^{z}=1 sectors is wrong, which sits at the second allowed value for these two sectors. Furthermore, the degeneracy of each level becomes poor. Nevertheless, we suspect that increasing the bond dimension and potentially adding more wires may help improve the results.

We also obtain the entanglement spectra for both ψ1\psi_{1} and ψs\psi_{s} associated with the three-chain cylinder (Fig. 24). Due to the small circumference, one cannot unambiguously identify the chirality or degeneracy pattern. Still, the spectra are consistent with the theoretical expectations.

E.4 Results at a different bond dimension for N=5,6N=5,6

The data for five- and six-chain systems in the main text come solely from MPSs at bond dimension χ=2000\chi=2000. In contrast, we obtained a series of infinite MPSs during VUMPS simulations for N=3,4N=3,4 and confirmed convergence by looking at correlation lengths and entanglement entropy. To support that the results for N=5,6N=5,6 are already faithful, we include measurements of the same quantities as shown in the main text using MPSs at χ=1000\chi=1000.

First, we examine the entanglement spectra for ψ1\psi_{1} and ψs\psi_{s} in a five-chain systems at bond dimension χ=1000\chi=1000 (Fig. 25). The low-lying states exhibit the expected pattern of a Laughlin state. Noticeable differences with Fig. 9 at χ=2000\chi=2000 occur at higher levels in the spectra. In particular, the χ=2000\chi=2000 spectra have eigenvalues associated with definite transverse momenta at entanglement energy −ln⁡((s2))≳10-\ln{(s^2)}\gtrsim 10. These eigenvalues get mixed with each other when we resolve kyk_{y} at χ=1000\chi=1000. Thus, we exclude them from Fig. 25.

Second, we evaluate the order parameters for spontaneous symmetry breakings using states at χ=1000\chi=1000. The data also exhibit the same symmetry-breaking behaviors. In Fig. 26, we show the relative difference between the two sets of data: one is at bond dimension χ=1000\chi=1000, and the other one corresponds to Fig. 10. The maximal relative difference of ⟨𝒪Dimer⟩\expectationvalue{\mathcal{O}_{\text{Dimer}}} near the system’s center is around 0.3%0.3\%, and the same maximal relative error for ⟨𝒪𝒫​𝒯⟩\expectationvalue{\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}}} is around 3%3\%.

Finally, we perform the flux insertion at χ=1000\chi=1000 for the XC-6(0) cylinder (Fig. 27). As anticipated, the spin transferred from one edge to the other is still precisely 1/21/2. At the same time, the MPS ψ⁡(Φ)\psi(\Phi) evolves from the semion sector to the identity sector. We note that the difference between the two sets of data (χ=1000,2000\chi=1000,2000) in the first panel of Fig. 27 is small, while the difference in the second panel is negligible.
